Jimmy Carter. The thirty-ninth President of the United States, serving from nineteen seventy-seven to nineteen eighty-one. A Democrat known for his focus on human rights, diplomacy, and moral principle in foreign policy, though his presidency was marked by economic stagnation, the Iran hostage crisis, and Cold War tensions that he struggled to manage. After leaving office, Carter became an influential elder statesman and humanitarian.

He was an outsider to conventional politics, a former nuclear engineer and Georgia governor who won the presidency in nineteen seventy-six on a platform of integrity and reform following Watergate and Vietnam. His greatest diplomatic triumph was the Camp David Accords in nineteen seventy-eight, where he brokered peace between Israel and Egypt, bringing Anwar Sadat and Menachem Begin to a historic accord that reshaped Middle Eastern geopolitics. Yet his presidency was defined by catastrophe abroad. The Iranian Revolution in nineteen seventy-nine and the subsequent hostage crisis saw American embassy staff held for four hundred forty-four days, a humiliation that dominated his presidency and contributed to his electoral defeat. The crisis was resolved only after Ronald Reagan's inauguration.

Carter championed human rights as a cornerstone of foreign policy, criticizing Soviet violations and other authoritarian regimes, earning respect from dissidents but generating friction with strategic allies. When the Soviet Union invaded Afghanistan in nineteen seventy-nine, Cold War escalation made détente impossible. Carter imposed grain embargoes and advocated a boycott of the nineteen eighty Moscow Olympics in protest. His domestic presidency struggled with stagflation, the simultaneous high inflation and unemployment that plagued the economy, and energy crises, particularly oil shocks. He lost re-election decisively to Reagan in nineteen eighty. After leaving office, Carter pursued Habitat for Humanity work and election monitoring, becoming the longest-living former president and aging into an elder statesman role. He shares important connections with the Camp David Accords, his signature diplomatic achievement brokering Arab-Israeli peace, with the Cold War itself, which coincided with détente's collapse and Soviet assertiveness, with Ronald Reagan, who defeated him and represented a different Cold War approach, with the Iran hostage crisis that defined and damaged his presidency, and with the Soviet Union, whose expansion marked the end of détente.
